ChineseWorkplace & Life案例 — 384 Lines
001 Yao H01 Qian Line 1 Build your skills before asking for prom▶

001 初九 | Build your skills before asking for promotion

001爻 line_id: XLIFE-H01-L1 xiang_id: XIANG-U-01-02 event_id: LIFE-E01

Xiao Xiang original | 潛龍勿用，陽在下也。

Xiao Xiang English | The hidden dragon should not act: the yang force remains below.

Historical event | TSMC establishes the dedicated foundry model

Interpretive analogy | Social post [174 English words]

Build your skills before asking for promotion. The Xiao Xiang says: “The hidden dragon should not act: the yang force remains below.” The historical comparison here concerns TSMC establishes the dedicated foundry model. In that event, the company needed factory equipment, process specialists, confidentiality, production scheduling, and customers willing to hand over their designs. The model gave designers an alternative to owning fabrication facilities.

What does that sequence suggest for a workplace or household decision? A new professional undertaking requires competence, timing, and an account of whom the work will serve. The practical reminder is to build your skills before asking for promotion. Before proceeding, separate a stated intention from the actions actually completed and the effects on other people. A convincing announcement is not the same thing as an implemented decision.

Write down one small action you can complete now, the information you still lack, and the person who can check your result. The historical comparison is retrospective. It does not establish that anyone in the episode consulted this particular commentary before acting.

Historical narrative reference: LIFE-E01 (see Part II)

Evidence class: B | Original source IDs: ETSMC

Original comparison (Traditional Chinese): 台積電成立時，把「替客戶製造、不與客戶競爭」確立為業務方向。乾卦的開創，不只靠衝勁；在職場選擇新路時，先想清楚自己要解決誰的問題、承諾能否長期兌現。「潛龍勿用，陽在下也」點出要看行動所處的位置。回到日常決策，起步先補齊技能，別急著要求升職。把已能獨立完成的工作、缺少的技能和需要的支援分開記錄，再決定下一步。這是後人拿史事對讀爻文，沒有史料說當事人依這一爻作決定。

002 Yao H01 Qian Line 2 Make your work useful to colleagues▶

002 九二 | Make your work useful to colleagues

002爻 line_id: XLIFE-H01-L2 xiang_id: XIANG-U-01-03 event_id: WENTAX

Xiao Xiang original | 見龍在田，德施普也。

Xiao Xiang English | The dragon appearing in the field: virtue spreads widely.

Historical event | Emperor Wen abolishes the Han land tax

Interpretive analogy | Social post [167 English words]

Make your work useful to colleagues. The Xiao Xiang says: “The dragon appearing in the field: virtue spreads widely.” The historical comparison here concerns Emperor Wen abolishes the Han land tax. In that event, in 167 BCE, Emperor Wen ordered the abolition of the land tax. The Book of Han records the measure in its account of the reign.

What does that sequence suggest for a workplace or household decision? A new professional undertaking requires competence, timing, and an account of whom the work will serve. The practical reminder is to make your work useful to colleagues. Before proceeding, separate a stated intention from the actions actually completed and the effects on other people. A convincing announcement is not the same thing as an implemented decision.

Identify who will use the result. Ask that person what a useful delivery looks like and record the agreed date. The event offers a situation to examine, not a rule that guarantees the same outcome in a different workplace or family.

Historical narrative reference: WENTAX (see Part II)

Evidence class: B | Original source IDs: HS24A

Original comparison (Traditional Chinese): 漢文帝免田租，使政策利益向農業生產者延伸，讓人想到德施於眾；仍需分辨有田與無田者。回看「見龍在田，德施普也」，還須留意事件前後的條件。對今天的工作與生活，能獨立交付後，讓成果真正幫到同事。請相關的人確認目標、交付日期與責任歸屬，避免每個人都以為別人會完成。這段歷史可供對照，不能因此推稱當事人曾用《小象》規劃行動。

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1987, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company was established. At the time, chip design and chip fabrication were frequently carried out by the same company. The new business offered to manufacture chips designed by other firms, rather than compete with its customers in designing products. The initial situation did not resolve itself through a title, proclamation, or single favorable moment. The people and institutions involved had to operate within the resources and responsibilities already present. What happened next therefore depended on practical steps, including how the proposed arrangement would be carried out in the setting described by the source.

The company needed factory equipment, process specialists, confidentiality, production scheduling, and customers willing to hand over their designs. Orders had to become test runs and then repeatable deliveries. Its division of labor was implemented through everyday production work, not by the founding announcement alone. Implementation was a separate part of the sequence. The action described in the record had to reach the people, organizations, or transactions concerned. Its consequences could only emerge through what was actually done, not through the wording of the plan alone. The account does not provide an individual scene for every participant, so no such scenes are added here.

The model gave designers an alternative to owning fabrication facilities. As processes and customer needs changed, continued investment, training, and quality management remained necessary. The corporate history does not document any decision made on the basis of the Xiao Xiang. The later situation should not be treated as proof that every participant benefited equally. The surviving record identifies the broad result, while leaving some local or individual consequences outside its scope. The event can therefore be followed from the original conditions, through the recorded action, to what came afterward without filling those gaps with imagined detail. The available material gives the reader an identifiable beginning, an intervening course of action, and a subsequent condition. Those stages should be kept distinct: the need that prompted action is not itself an outcome, and a later outcome does not establish every detail of how participants experienced the change. The account is limited to the circumstances, actions, and consequences recorded for this event.

Historical event | Short narrative

The Records of the Grand Historian describes the Cao Bing family as having built a business from iron production. Smelting and dealing in iron could create income, but an established workshop did not by itself determine how household wealth would be retained or used. The family had to make choices about everyday spending and the deployment of resources beyond its original line of work.

The account describes a combination of ironworking, frugal household habits, lending, and commerce across places. Income from production was not treated as identical to money available for unlimited consumption. The family kept expenditure under restraint while engaging in other transactions. Lending moved resources to borrowers and created the possibility of repayment or default. Trade across localities required merchandise to circulate between markets, where transport and changes in demand mattered.

These activities were not one instantaneous act of investment. They formed a sequence in which productive work provided a foundation, household management affected the amount retained, and lending or trade opened additional channels for circulating wealth. The historical text summarizes the family’s economic conduct rather than presenting modern accounts with individual loan rates, trading dates, costs, or yearly returns. It would therefore be inaccurate to calculate an annualized investment performance from this story.

The resulting family wealth is presented in the historical account, but its size should not be used to infer that every loan or shipment yielded a profit. The enduring point of the chronology is that the household’s production, expenses, and commercial dealings remained connected over time. Expanding each sector without arranging their respective roles would not automatically resolve these shortages. Public economic planning therefore had to address the order in which investments and supporting production could take place.

Beginning in 1953, Taiwan implemented its first Four-Year Economic Development Plan. The plan linked agricultural development with selected light industries and promoted some forms of import-substituting production. Its approach was not to make all industries self-sufficient immediately. Agriculture and industry were treated as sectors whose outputs and demands could support each other if resources were allocated in a practicable sequence. Plans were established across years rather than executed as a single purchase or construction project.

As the planning period unfolded, public investment had to be allocated and producers had to adjust within the available conditions. Farms and industrial enterprises did not change their operations at exactly the same time. In 1949, many Taiwanese tenant farmers cultivated land belonging to landlords. Rent took a portion of the crops they produced, so the terms of tenancy shaped how much of the harvest remained available for household needs. Government officials sought to alter these terms through a policy known as the 37.5 Percent Rent Reduction. The problem involved distribution between owners and cultivators as well as the enforceability of their agreements.

Beginning in 1949, the authorities introduced rent-reduction measures intended to lower the burden on tenant farmers and protect cultivation rights. The policy changed the framework under which landowners and tenants shared the outcome of farming. It was not merely a statement that tenant livelihoods should improve. Rental terms had to be reflected in actual leases and local administration. Changes in the rental share affected the income received by landlords and the portion retained by the people working the land.

After the rule changed, both sides still had ongoing obligations. Farmers had to continue cultivating and landlords retained property interests that were not wholly resolved by lower rent. The supplied archival account identifies the reform’s purpose and implementation period, but it does not list the before-and-after income of every affected family. Nor does it establish that all disputes over landownership disappeared when rent was reduced. Those matters require separate records for particular districts and contracts.

The event therefore proceeds from a pre-existing pattern of tenancy, through a legal change in rental distribution, into the practical renegotiation of rights and obligations. Its documented outcome is a change in rental arrangements and protections, not a uniform financial result for every household. Source trace: LAND, the account of the policy introduced in 1949.

Historical event | Short narrative

During the Warring States period, the ruler of Qin proposed exchanging cities for the Heshi jade disk held by Zhao. The proposal created a diplomatic problem. Sending the object might leave Zhao without either the jade or the promised territory. Refusing Qin, a much stronger state, also carried risks. Zhao therefore appointed Lin Xiangru to travel to the Qin court with the jade and conduct the exchange.

After arriving, Lin Xiangru presented the object and observed that Qin had not immediately provided the promised cities. According to the Records of the Grand Historian, he obtained the jade back by offering to point out a flaw in it. He then challenged the manner in which the exchange was being handled and sought more formal conditions for the transfer. The surviving biography recounts an extended confrontation, including speeches. Because these speeches come through a later historian, their exact wording should not be treated as a verbatim transcript.

As discussions continued, Lin Xiangru arranged for the jade to be returned to Zhao. He remained at the Qin court to face the consequences. This separated the immediate task of safeguarding the object from the unresolved diplomatic dispute. The proposed exchange of cities for the jade was not completed. Qin did not obtain the object under the original terms, and Zhao did not receive the cities.

The episode can be followed from Qin's proposal, through Zhao's appointment of an envoy and the negotiations at court, to the return of the jade. It is a narrative preserved in the Shiji biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru, not a contemporary transcript of every meeting. The manuscript uses it as a retrospective comparison for a workplace decision about choosing a suitable course under unequal bargaining power. It does not provide evidence that Lin Xiangru consulted this Xiao Xiang commentary.

In 1983, Hong Kong experienced pressure on the value of its currency and on confidence in monetary arrangements. Shopkeepers setting prices and households holding cash needed a reasonably comprehensible way of making payments. When expectations about the Hong Kong dollar became unsettled, businesses also faced difficulties organizing receipts and expenditures involving different currencies. The currency question thus reached daily transactions as well as financial markets.

On 17 October 1983, Hong Kong introduced the Linked Exchange Rate System. The arrangement set a defined framework linking the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar through arrangements governing note issuance and convertibility. Its introduction gave banks and market participants an explicit set of operating rules rather than relying only on public expressions of confidence. The date marks the beginning of the arrangement, not proof that every participant immediately regained confidence.

Once the framework was announced, participating institutions had to continue operating according to it. Currency issuance, conversion practices, and subsequent transactions were the mechanisms through which the arrangement became part of economic life. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s historical account records the introduction and institutional design. It does not report what every merchant decided on the day of implementation or establish an identical effect for all businesses.

The sequence is therefore one of uncertainty, an announced monetary framework, and continuing operation under the new rules. A policy date can be established precisely while changes in confidence require observation across later transactions. Source trace: LINK, the account dating the system to 17 October 1983.

During the Asian financial crisis, Hong Kong's equity and currency markets came under pressure. The government faced the question of whether public money should be deployed in share purchases. Either intervention or non-intervention involved potential consequences for market participants and for public assets. The choice could not be assessed solely by the immediate movement in share prices.

In 1998, the Hong Kong government entered the stock market and purchased shares. Official annual reports describe this action as a response to attacks on the financial market. That is the public authority's stated justification, while the boundary between market stabilization and public intervention remained a subject of debate. The purchase transformed a temporary market action into an ongoing responsibility to hold, account for, and eventually dispose of the acquired securities.

The government could not stop managing these assets at the close of the trading day. A portfolio acquired using public resources required custody, valuation, and decisions about eventual transfer to the market. The related 1999 Tracker Fund was one subsequent mechanism for disposing of part of the shares, but it should not be confused with the decision taken in 1998. The official account supplies the policy setting and broad chronology, not a transaction-by-transaction audit of all public costs or an uncontested judgement of the intervention.

Source caveat: 這是長期變化的概述，不表示所有地區同樣富裕，也不證明君主按泰卦施政。

Historical event | Short narrative

After the civil conflicts surrounding the beginning of the Han dynasty, agriculture and public revenues had to be restored over time. Cultivation, tax collection, and the management of grain and money were connected: the treasury could accumulate reserves only as a functioning productive base returned. A government with more stored resources could meet administrative needs and some unexpected demands without immediately seeking new funds.

The Book of Han describes the accumulation of considerable state stores following years of recovery. Grain stocks and public money grew during the period associated with Emperors Wen and Jing and the early Han period that followed. Such stores represented resources built up across multiple seasons and fiscal decisions. They were not the result of a single deposit made on one day or a guarantee that future expenditure would remain small.

The historical account also records a later change as major state spending increased, including under Emperor Wu. Public resources that had accumulated previously were drawn upon as obligations expanded. Earlier abundance and later fiscal pressure therefore belong to different stages of the sequence. It would misrepresent the narrative to describe the treasury as simultaneously accumulating and exhausting the same reserves at the same moment.

The episode proceeds from postwar recovery to stronger public stores and then to new spending pressures that reduced fiscal room. The cited sections establish the broad historical movement, not a modern consolidated budget with annual balances for every office. The amount available at one time could not alone determine what later commitments would cost. Source trace: HS24A and HS24B, the descriptions of accumulated treasury resources and later expenditures.

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1978, farming households in Xiaogang village, Anhui, faced problems of agricultural production and household subsistence. The existing collective arrangements did not make the connection between each household’s work and its share of production sufficiently clear for the families seeking change. The villagers’ response was to write down a different division of responsibility rather than simply announce a higher production target. The surviving document provides a concrete record of a local attempt to reorganize agricultural work.

Eighteen farming households signed an agreement commonly described as baogan daohu, or contracting production responsibilities to households. The document assigned households the work they had to undertake and the obligations they had to deliver. Its practical significance lay in identifying who was responsible for cultivating the land and fulfilling the agreed deliveries. Signing the agreement did not produce a harvest. The families still had to cultivate fields, handle the agricultural season, and carry out their undertakings after the document was made.

The contract subsequently became part of accounts of China's rural reform, but this later significance should not be projected back onto the moment of signing. The local experiment and the later diffusion of household responsibility arrangements were different stages. The preserved artifact confirms the attempt by the eighteen households; it does not contain a complete season-by-season ledger showing each family's output, income, or later position. The historical sequence is therefore limited but clear: households confronted livelihood problems, set down a new allocation of responsibilities, and then had to put that allocation into practice.

The story ends not with an instant national transformation but with an identifiable village agreement entering a longer history of changes in agricultural organization. The question of how far this local approach could be extended belonged to subsequent policies and subsequent evidence. Source trace: XIAO, the account of the eighteen-household contract.

In China during the early 1930s, silver remained closely connected to currency, banking, and settlement of payments. Banks and businesses depended on the availability of the metal within the domestic financial system. Changes in international silver markets and foreign policy altered demand for silver outside China, creating pressure for silver to flow out of the country.

From about 1933 to 1935, the movement of silver became a financial concern. The outflow placed pressure on bank liquidity and on businesses that depended upon credit and reliable settlement. Institutions including the Bank of China attempted to coordinate responses. Yet the difficulty arose from the interaction between world-market prices and China's domestic currency arrangements. A single bank, merchant, or local office could not remove the international incentives underlying the movement of the metal.

The issue did not end with an isolated banking decision. Subsequent monetary reform changed the relationship between silver and the new legal-tender system, forming a later institutional response to the crisis. Banking histories preserve the sequence of financial pressure, coordination, and policy change, but do not identify an identical shortage in every city or provide complete bank-by-bank accounts. Precise silver prices, quantities shipped, and individual losses would need separate statistical verification. The documented story therefore runs from an external market shift, through domestic monetary stress and attempts at coordination, to a broader reform of the currency framework. It should not be reduced to one day's price movement.

The available material identifies major actions and their sequence, not every participant's individual choices. Any more precise figures, private conversations, motives, or household-level outcomes would require evidence beyond the cited account. The story is accordingly confined to the measures and consequences actually described in the source, without presenting a later historical analogy as something the historical actors themselves said or believed. In this account, the initial problem, the recorded intervention, and the subsequent responsibility are distinguishable phases. No unrecorded conversation or psychological explanation is needed to establish that chronology.

In 635 BCE, disorder within the Zhou royal house forced King Xiang of Zhou away from his capital. Duke Wen of Jin had already established a position among the regional lords. His adviser Hu Yan urged assistance to the Zhou king, presenting the matter as both a response to the royal crisis and an opportunity for Jin to strengthen its standing.

The Zuo Zhuan records that Duke Wen consulted divination and received the hexagram Da You changing to Kui. The transmitted interpretation included wording associated with the Son of Heaven. This consultation belongs to the recorded sequence, but it was not the only step. Jin still had to decide on action, organize military support and carry out the intervention. The surviving narrative describes political advice, divination and military action together; it does not reduce the operation to a prediction automatically producing its result.

Jin subsequently sent forces to help King Xiang return to the royal capital. Following the restoration, Jin received rewards. These developments changed Jin's relationship to the Zhou court and formed part of the broader political settlement. The reward was an aftermath of the intervention, not evidence that divination guaranteed success or that all possible costs had been removed.

The account is preserved in the Zuo Zhuan for the twenty-fifth year of Duke Xi of Lu, with a parallel tradition in the Xin Xu. The transmitted wordings differ in some places, including forms commonly rendered heng and xiang. Grain prices in the frontier commanderies of the Western Han empire changed with harvests and the availability of supplies. Farmers could receive low prices when grain was abundant, while buyers faced higher costs in short periods. If public authorities waited for a shortage before seeking food, procurement and transport would take additional time when demand was already pressing.

Geng Shouchang proposed establishing ever-normal granaries, or changpingcang, in which grain could be purchased when prices were low and sold when prices were high. This arrangement was designed to link storage with market conditions. By buying, keeping, and later releasing grain, the administration could hold stock between seasons rather than attempt all procurement during a shortage. Farmers selling after a harvest and households buying during scarcity were affected at different points in the cycle.

Granaries required upkeep and decisions as well as grain. Stocks had to be protected from loss, and officials needed to decide when to purchase or release them. The Book of Han describes the proposal and its operating principle, but does not establish that every granary in every year adjusted prices accurately or benefited all participants in the same degree. The sequence is a recognized problem with fluctuating prices, a proposal to acquire and store reserves, and later sales in response to demand. Storage converted an immediate purchase into the possibility of a future supply; the usefulness of that reserve still depended on maintenance and timing.

During the Northern Song dynasty, reforms introduced under the preceding emperor altered the way the government raised and collected revenue. Among the contested measures were the service-related payments commonly called exemption money. The measures had political significance because they were associated with an earlier ruler. Anyone proposing to change them also had to address whether revising an inherited policy amounted to rejecting that ruler's intentions. The argument therefore concerned both the burdens of fiscal administration and the responsibilities of political succession.

In 1085, Sima Guang submitted a memorial discussing the new policies. He cited two passages from the Xiao Xiang commentary on Hexagram 18, Gu: one accompanying the first line and the other accompanying the fourth line. In his argument, the passages helped distinguish responsible correction of an earlier policy from passive preservation of an inherited arrangement. He urged that policies harmful to the people and the state should not be maintained merely because they had been adopted by a previous emperor. The quotations belong to the documented reasoning of the memorial, not to an interpretation assigned to Sima Guang by a modern reader.

The memorial can establish what Sima Guang argued, which passages he quoted, and the policy question he was addressing. It does not, by itself, establish the financial effects of every provision he opposed. Nor does a quotation from a classical text prove that the ensuing policy outcome was beneficial. Those are different historical questions, requiring administrative records and evidence beyond the memorial's own advocacy.

The sequence is thus specific: the new fiscal measures were introduced; disputes arose over their consequences and their connection to an earlier reign; Sima Guang submitted a memorial in 1085 and quoted the Xiao Xiang while calling for reconsideration. The later operation and results of the measures must be evaluated separately. The surviving text records an actual use of the commentary in a fiscal-policy dispute, while leaving the wider evidence about implementation and outcomes open to investigation.

In 158 BCE, Emperor Wen of Han inspected military camps while troops were stationed to protect the capital region. Earlier stops had allowed the imperial party relatively easy passage. The inspection consequently began with a delay at the entrance.

The imperial attendants communicated with the camp, and entry was granted after the required authorization. The contrast with the other inspected camps is central to the way the historian portrays Zhou Yafu's command.

It does not establish that the emperor followed the same procedure on every occasion or that all military commands were always implemented fairly. No passage in this episode records Emperor Wen consulting the Xiao Xiang commentary on the hexagram Lin.

By 1948, the Nationalist government faced civil war, serious monetary depreciation, and continuing pressure on public finances and supplies. Existing money had become difficult to rely upon for everyday transactions. Households held savings in a changing monetary environment, while merchants needed a unit in which to quote prices and settle purchases. The government introduced a replacement currency as part of an attempt to restore a functioning payment system.

The Gold Yuan was issued in 1948. Citizens and businesses had to adjust their money holdings and accounting to the new currency arrangements. The issue of new notes altered the official medium of payment, but the underlying wartime fiscal strains and supply problems continued. As the currency circulated, its purchasing power fell rapidly. The new unit did not reverse the depreciation that had made reform necessary.

In 1949 the Gold Yuan ceased to circulate. Holders of the currency had experienced further losses of purchasing power as the promised new medium failed to maintain its value. Museum and collection accounts establish the principal issue and withdrawal dates, though they do not provide a complete monthly price series for every product or the losses of every household. The record follows a clear progression: a deteriorating older currency, the government's issuance and adoption of a replacement, continuing pressures on finances and goods, and the replacement's rapid loss of value and eventual withdrawal. Changing the printed unit did not itself resolve the conditions affecting what the money could purchase.

The available material identifies major actions and their sequence, not every participant's individual choices. Any more precise figures, private conversations, motives, or household-level outcomes would require evidence beyond the cited account. The story is accordingly confined to the measures and consequences actually described in the source, without presenting a later historical analogy as something the historical actors themselves said or believed.

The story ends not with an instant national transformation but with an identifiable village agreement entering a longer history of changes in agricultural organization. Near the end of the Spring and Autumn period, King Zhao of Chu fell ill. The Zuo Zhuan, in its account under the sixth year of Duke Ai of Lu, records a divination that connected the illness with the Yellow River. Officials proposed a sacrifice to the river deity. The suggestion arose within the ritual and divinatory practices of the period, when a ruler's illness could prompt questions about obligations to supernatural powers. It was also a matter of state ceremony, since the king's acts had to conform to the accepted boundaries of Chu's rites.

King Zhao did not authorize the proposed sacrifice. The account attributes to him an explanation that sacrifices prescribed by earlier dynasties were not to extend beyond the relevant territory. He identified the Jiang, Han, Ju and Zhang rivers as the waters associated with Chu's ritual sphere. The Yellow River was outside that sphere. Although the ruler acknowledged that he might have shortcomings, he rejected the suggestion that he should offer to a river beyond Chu's established ritual responsibility. The ministers' proposed remedy was therefore not carried out.

The passage also preserves a separate account of an ominous celestial appearance and advice that a ritual might transfer danger from the king to senior officials. King Zhao rejected that transfer as well. These episodes appear in the same transmitted historical narrative, but they should not be collapsed into a single divination or described as evidence of a modern medical treatment. The record describes the proposals and the king's responses, not a clinical explanation of the illness.

King Zhao later died while campaigning to assist Chen. The account of the river sacrifice does not show that refusing the rite caused or prevented his death. What can be traced is the initial illness, the proposal for an exceptional sacrifice, the king's refusal on grounds of ritual jurisdiction, and the absence of the proposed rite. That limitation remains important when the episode is paired with a present-day discussion of responsibility and decision-making.

The manuscript directs readers to the materials identified as TEN2 and CBC for Taiwan's economic and monetary context during the 1970s.

After the An Lushan Rebellion, the Tang court needed to move grain and other goods from the Jianghuai region toward Guanzhong. Supplies could exist in producing areas while the capital region still faced difficulty receiving them. Disruption to waterways, transport administration and the connections between collection and delivery made the journey as important as the amount collected. The state had to provide for soldiers and civilians, while its revenue system also depended on moving material resources.

In the later eighth century, Liu Yan worked to reorganize waterborne transport. The historical account links his measures with taxation, civilian supply and military provisions. He addressed how goods could move along the route rather than treating the supply problem as a single decision to collect more grain. Collection, loading, navigation, unloading and delivery required coordinated work. Even where a waterway could be used, the goods needed to pass between people and offices responsible for different stages. The record describes improvements to transport and its administration, but does not provide the itinerary, cargo and delivery date of every boat.

As these arrangements were improved, the movement of goods toward Guanzhong became more workable. The account presents this as part of the effort to restore supply after the rebellion. It does not establish that every shortage ended, or that a single measure accounted for all changes in state finances. Boats still required crews, waterways needed attention and deliveries had to be accounted for after the initial reform.

The sequence is therefore a postwar supply problem, an administrative effort to restore the transport connection, and a more functional route for moving goods toward those who needed them. The historical material supports that sequence and the broad purpose of Liu Yan's work. It does not preserve a complete series of shipping ledgers from which to calculate each voyage's cost or profit. The case illustrates a practical distinction between having resources at their point of origin and ensuring that they arrive at their destination.

Before the Shanghai Stock Exchange opened, securities transactions in China did not yet have the same organized marketplace, common procedures and public timetable that an exchange could provide. Investors and institutions needed ways to identify what was being traded, obtain prices and carry out transactions under rules that participants could recognize. A market is not simply a place where buyers and sellers gather. It also depends on how orders are recorded, transactions are completed and relevant information is made available. The source manuscript identifies the need for a more organized trading venue as the background to the new institution.

The Shanghai Stock Exchange was established in 1990 and formally opened for business on 19 December that year. Its creation provided an institutional setting for centralized securities trading. This marked a specific organizational change, not the immediate completion of every rule required for a mature market. Participants could come together around a trading venue, while the exchange and relevant authorities still needed to address the procedures used in listing, transactions, disclosure and supervision. The opening date is documented in the exchange's institutional history. That history does not provide a complete record of every trade executed by every investor.

After the exchange began operating, the work of organizing a securities market continued. Listed companies and market participants had to follow evolving requirements, while investors remained exposed to changes in security prices and the circumstances of individual companies. A common trading venue could make some procedures more consistent, but it did not remove the risk of losses. Nor does the existence of an exchange prove that every security was fairly valued or that every investor received the same result.

The sequence is therefore a demand for a more organized trading system, the establishment and opening of the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 1990, and the subsequent operation and development of market rules and oversight. These are the stages supported by the manuscript's reference to the exchange's official history. No unrecorded trading conversations, personal motives or precise investment returns are needed to tell the story. The institution's founding was an identifiable event; the effectiveness of its continuing operations is a separate subject for historical examination.

Historical event | Short narrative

The Records of the Grand Historian includes the merchant Shi Shi of Luoyang among accounts of people who accumulated wealth through commerce. The source describes a business that did not depend solely on one shop or a single local market. Goods had to be moved between places, and that movement required both transport and people capable of handling transactions. For a merchant operating beyond familiar streets, distance created opportunities to reach buyers, but it also separated the owner from the daily work of buying, carrying, and selling.

Shi Shi organized trading journeys and made use of experienced assistants. Carts, goods, and entrusted workers were parts of the same undertaking. People traveling with merchandise needed to understand the route and the markets they encountered. The merchant could not personally oversee every stage in every place. Delegating work therefore mattered as much as having goods available to trade. The source emphasizes this organization and the resulting commercial success, without providing a full schedule of journeys.

As the journeys proceeded, the arrangements had to work in more than one setting. Transport linked the places where merchandise was obtained and the places where it could be sold. Those who acted on the merchant's behalf needed sufficient knowledge to carry out transactions in his absence. The surviving account gives the broad pattern of this activity rather than individual invoices, exact sale prices, or a complete record of payments. It does not identify a particular storm, robbery, or negotiation that can be turned into a dramatic scene.

The recorded outcome is that Shi Shi appears in the historian's discussion of prosperous merchants. That placement indicates how the source regarded his commercial activity, but it cannot establish the results of every journey or the circumstances of every worker. The sequence that can be responsibly retold is the formation of a trading operation, the dispatch of goods and capable personnel across regions, and the subsequent reputation for commercial success. It is a story of documented organization and movement, not a guarantee that leaving one's home market produces wealth.

During the Warring States period, the court of Qi faced the familiar problem of how a ruler could hear criticism from people whose positions depended on him. The Zhanguo ce introduces this problem through a domestic episode involving Zou Ji. He asked his wife, a concubine and a visiting guest to compare his appearance with that of Xu Gong, a man known for his looks. Each answer favored Zou Ji. Their responses sounded consistent, but the people giving them did not occupy the same relationship to him.

When Zou Ji later saw Xu Gong, he judged that the favorable comparisons had not been reliable. The narrative explains the answers by reference to affection, apprehension and the hope of obtaining something. Zou Ji then took the example to King Wei of Qi. The point of his presentation was not to settle a contest of appearances. He described how the people surrounding a ruler might likewise withhold unwelcome judgments because of their dependence on him. The king's position made that problem potentially larger than the one within a household.

The account says that King Wei accepted the advice and announced rewards for different forms of remonstrance. Criticism delivered directly, written submissions and remarks circulating in public were given places within the arrangement. The narrative subsequently describes the number of remonstrances changing over time and presents the court as better able to receive information. These developments form the story's aftermath, as told in the text.

The Zhanguo ce is a collection shaped by persuasive rhetoric, not a transcript of each exchange. The dialogue and the reported progression of remonstrances should be read with that literary character in mind. In particular, fewer recorded complaints cannot establish that every difficulty in Qi had disappeared. What the surviving account preserves is a sequence: favorable answers in a household, a comparison that exposed their limitations, a presentation to the king and an announced channel for criticism. It does not show that Zou Ji or King Wei consulted the later Xiao Xiang commentary.

In 81 BCE, during the reign of Emperor Zhao of the Western Han, the court convened discussions about economic policies associated with the preceding reign. Government monopolies in salt and iron and related arrangements for moving and selling goods had become matters of controversy. State officials defended the resources these policies supplied for frontier defense and public expenditure. Scholars and other critics raised the effects on farmers, merchants and ordinary households. The two sides did not begin with the same measure of what counted as a benefit.

The discussion brought these positions into a shared forum. One argument concerned the revenue needed to maintain military commitments and administration. Another concerned prices, local livelihoods and the burden of government participation in commerce. When speakers discussed profit or public welfare, they sometimes referred to different beneficiaries and different time horizons. Questions could therefore be answered by disputing the assumptions behind them rather than by accepting a common set of figures. The exchanges also reflected unequal positions: participants were invited to speak, but they did not possess equal authority to determine policy.

The work known as the Yantie lun, or Discourses on Salt and Iron, later preserved an organized account of the arguments. It presents speakers responding to each other over multiple topics and lets later readers follow the lines of disagreement. The text is a literary and editorial record of debate, not an unedited stenographic transcript. It cannot establish the exact wording, duration or reception of every contribution at the meeting. Nor can one infer that the debate ended with complete agreement or immediate repeal of every disputed measure.

The documented sequence begins with established policies and criticism of their consequences, moves to a court-sponsored exchange of competing arguments and continues in a written record that circulated afterward. The surviving work makes the competing claims visible, while leaving the precise influence of particular speeches on subsequent decisions a separate historical question. This episode is paired with the Xiao Xiang retrospectively; the sources do not connect the participants' reasoning to that commentary.

Original Chinese title: 法幣改革整合分散支付制度 | Period: 1935年｜近現代｜本稿對照1次

Original source codes: EFABI、ETWO2

Source location: 1935年11月4日報告所錄改革措施

Source caveat: 法幣後來也面臨嚴重通膨，不能把建立共同規則等同永久成功。

Historical event | Short narrative

By the early 1930s, China's monetary system was under pressure from movements in the international price and supply of silver. Banks, merchants and households relied on payment arrangements that had to work across different places and contracts. As silver left the country and financial conditions tightened, continuing with existing practices became increasingly difficult. A currency reform could be announced centrally, but the practical change would still have to pass through bank counters, commercial accounts and everyday transactions.

In November 1935, the government announced the fabi reform. Banknotes issued by designated banks were established as legal currency, while rules concerning silver holdings and monetary arrangements were revised. The measures sought to bring payments into a more unified system. People and institutions holding silver had to consider the new requirements, and commercial parties had to decide how to settle obligations using the recognized means of payment. A legal declaration did not by itself complete every conversion or resolve every question of acceptance.

The next stage unfolded wherever money changed hands. Banks needed to apply the new rules to deposits and payments. Businesses needed to use the recognized currency when settling accounts, while individuals encountered the changes through wages, purchases and savings. The reform's intended coordination depended on these repeated transactions. Official announcements and contemporary reporting establish the date and broad measures, but they do not provide a complete record of how every locality or household adjusted.

The new arrangements provided a different basis for payment during the years that followed. They did not make the currency permanently stable. War, fiscal pressure and subsequent inflation severely weakened fabi in later years, and China eventually experienced further monetary changes. The story therefore runs from mounting pressure on the silver-based system, through the announcement and implementation of new payment rules, to later difficulties that exposed the limits of reform. Its use beside the Xiao Xiang is an editorial comparison, not evidence that the reformers consulted that commentary.

In the fourth century BCE, the Qin state prepared to introduce legal reforms associated with Shang Yang under Duke Xiao. According to the account, a pole three zhang long was placed near the southern gate of the capital's marketplace. An announcement offered ten jin to anyone who carried it to the northern gate. No one initially accepted the task. The offered reward was then raised to fifty jin. One person moved the pole, and the promised fifty jin was paid. The text presents the payment as a visible demonstration that the announced terms would be honored. Only after this episode does the narrative say that the new laws were promulgated.

Grain prices in the frontier commanderies of the Western Han empire changed with harvests and the availability of supplies. Farmers could receive low prices when grain was abundant, while buyers faced higher costs in short periods. If public authorities waited for a shortage before seeking food, procurement and transport would take additional time when demand was already pressing.

Geng Shouchang proposed establishing ever-normal granaries, or changpingcang, in which grain could be purchased when prices were low and sold when prices were high. This arrangement was designed to link storage with market conditions. By buying, keeping, and later releasing grain, the administration could hold stock between seasons rather than attempt all procurement during a shortage. Farmers selling after a harvest and households buying during scarcity were affected at different points in the cycle.

Granaries required upkeep and decisions as well as grain. Stocks had to be protected from loss, and officials needed to decide when to purchase or release them. The Book of Han describes the proposal and its operating principle, but does not establish that every granary in every year adjusted prices accurately or benefited all participants in the same degree. The sequence is a recognized problem with fluctuating prices, a proposal to acquire and store reserves, and later sales in response to demand. Storage converted an immediate purchase into the possibility of a future supply; the usefulness of that reserve still depended on maintenance and timing.

The available material identifies major actions and their sequence, not every participant's individual choices. Any more precise figures, private conversations, motives, or household-level outcomes would require evidence beyond the cited account. The story is accordingly confined to the measures and consequences actually described in the source, without presenting a later historical analogy as something the historical actors themselves said or believed. In this account, the initial problem, the recorded intervention, and the subsequent responsibility are distinguishable phases. No unrecorded conversation or psychological explanation is needed to establish that chronology.

At the beginning of the twenty-first century, Taiwan faced the task of resolving problems at financial institutions whose condition threatened the continuity of banking services. A troubled institution could affect depositors, employees and the communities relying on its branches. Dealing with it required decisions about assets, liabilities and the transfer or termination of operations. In 2001, a financial restructuring fund was established to provide a legal mechanism for addressing such cases.

The fund operated through a defined period that extended to the end of 2011. Cases were not identical. Some institutions needed arrangements for another institution to assume business, while others required different forms of disposition. Depositors needed information about access to their funds, and the public needed an account of the use of the mechanism. Official material records that 56 troubled institutions were handled during the fund's period. That figure is an aggregate; it is not a complete history of the decision, cost and outcome for each institution.

The work continued beyond the initial identification of a problem. Legal procedures had to be followed, receiving institutions or other parties had to be identified where applicable, and the relevant records had to be preserved. The close of the authorized period supplied a point at which the program's scope and reported results could be reviewed. It did not mean that every future financial difficulty had been prevented, or that all issues affecting individual institutions ended on the same day.

The documented sequence begins with the creation of a public resolution mechanism, continues through the handling of individual troubled institutions and reaches a formal endpoint for the fund's designated period. Subsequent supervision, institutional learning and the management of new risks belong to continuing financial administration. The surviving official summary supports the dates, the mechanism and the reported total, but cannot substitute for detailed case records. The modern comparison with the Xiao Xiang concerns the difference between finishing one phase and eliminating all future uncertainty; it is not a claim about the motives of those who administered the fund.

Data model: Line(line_id, absolute_line_index, hexagram_number, line_label_zh, xiang_id, xiang_original_zh, xiang_en, social_post_en, event_id, evidence_class, source_ids, publication_status); Event(event_id, title_en, narrative_en, source_ids, source_locator, caveat, verification_status); Source(source_id, bibliographic_reference, verified_url). A line references one event, while multiple lines may reference the same event.

Use UTF-8 and locale keys zh-Hant and en. API: GET /api/v1/xiang/lines?from=1&to=384&locale=en; GET /api/v1/events/{event_id}?locale=en. Store paragraph boundaries; sanitize rich text; never construct URLs from opaque source identifiers. Maintain a content revision and separate historical verification and editorial approval statuses.

RWD: mobile <768 CSS px uses a single reading column and at least 16px body type; tablet 768–1199px uses a spacious reading column; desktop ≥1200px may show Chinese and English commentary side by side. Use 44px or larger touch targets, visible focus states, accessible disclosure controls and no fixed-height containers for long narratives. Display: hexagram and line → original commentary → English commentary → social post → linked historical story → sources and caveats.

Release checklist: 64 hexagrams × 6 lines, no missing or duplicate indices, stable IDs, all event references resolved, 150–200 English words per social post, 300–500 per historical story, no invented dialogue or motives, and source-by-source historical verification before public launch.
